description: We are The Shifters, a team of 6 uniting technology and agriculture. We're Computer Science & AI students from Alexandria University, Pharos University, and AASTMT, skilled in software development, coding, web development, AI, machine learning, data analysis, and visualization, integrated with Faculty of Agriculture, Alexandria University (Saba Basha). We're building a tool for smarter crop rotations and healthy soil
summary:
Journey Into the Soil is a web app that helps farmers and agronomists in Egypt choose crop rotations that hold up under a changing climate. The user picks a field on a map, or one of 27 demo sites, enters basic soil and crop details, and compares three rotation strategies.
NASA data sits at the core. Daily NASA POWER weather (2000-2025) drives a soil water and salinity simulation, and each rotation is replayed over 15 past years with optional warming and rainfall shifts, so results come as a range instead of one number. SMAP soil moisture and VIIRS NDVI are shown beside the model as an indicative check for the sites that have them. A 3D root-zone view and English/Arabic support make it easier to use.
It matters because water is limited, the climate is shifting, and most farmers don’t have access to this kind of analysis. The app gives estimates and risk ranges, not guarantees, and it labels any placeholder input as a data gap.
details:
What it does and how it works

Journey Into the Soil is a web app that helps farmers and agronomists in Egypt compare crop rotation plans. The user picks a field on a map, or one of 27 prebuilt demo sites, and answers a short four-step wizard about soil, irrigation, crop history and goals. The app then builds three plans: the existing rotation, the best plan for the user’s top priority, and a contrasting option.

Each plan is run through a physics-based simulation: FAO-56 evapotranspiration, Saxton-Rawls soil water properties, a four-layer soil water balance and a salinity yield penalty. Daily weather comes from NASA POWER (2000-2025). To show how plans behave in different kinds of years, we replay each one over 15 historical years (2011-2025), with optional warming and rainfall changes. The results come as ranges (low, typical, high) and as a rank stability figure, which shows how often a plan stays on top. For five demo sites, NASA SMAP soil moisture and VIIRS NDVI are shown next to the model as an indicative check. A 3D view of the root zone lets users see the soil layers.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers often choose the next crop without seeing water use, soil health and climate risk side by side. The app puts those in one view, in English and Arabic (including right-to-left layout). We want it to support better water management, more resilient crop choices and easier access to agronomic guidance. It gives estimates and risk ranges, not guarantees, and it is meant to support local expertise, not replace it.

Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, pytest
  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Babylon.js and Three.js (3D), MapLibre GL (map), i18next (English/Arabic)
  • Data: NASA POWER, SMAP (SPL3SMP_E), VIIRS NDVI (VNP13A1), ISRIC SoilGrids; optional Meteomatics live data
  • Knowledge assistant: BM25 keyword search over a bundled agronomy knowledge base, with citations. A LLM can rewrite the answer in plain language, but it never produces scores or rankings.
  • Deployment: Docker Compose

What is creative about it

It joins satellite data, soil physics and multi-year uncertainty in one tool that a farmer can use, and it shows the result inside the soil itself through the 3D dive. It also treats honesty as a feature: placeholder or unreviewed inputs are shown as data gaps and lower the confidence level, instead of being hidden.

Factors we considered

  • The demo works offline, using prebuilt data packs, so it does not depend on a connection.
  • All scores and rankings are calculated by equations and rules, so results can be checked and repeated.
  • Crop parameters are seeded from FAO tables and still need expert review. The app marks them as unreviewed.
  • Full Arabic support, since the users are Egyptian farmers.
  • Climate uncertainty: one weather year can mislead, so we use 15.
